learnings.title: Start Here: How to Use This Section
learnings.answer:
This is a field manual for one specific exam: the **HackerEarth frontend engineer test**, 2 hours, taken in HackerEarth's own in-browser IDE. It is not a React tutorial and not a JavaScript course — the app already has those. This section is about *converting what you know into points under a clock*.

## The shape of the thing

The practice test was 4 questions / 116 points / 45 minutes: 2 MCQ, 1 Subjective, 1 Project. The real test is 2 hours with the same question types. Read that ratio carefully — the Project question is worth roughly as much as everything else combined, several times over.

So the priority order for your remaining prep time is:

1. **Project archetypes** (entries 6-12) — this is where the points are
2. **Cold recall** (entries 13-17) — the IDE has no useful autocomplete, so anything you can't type from memory costs minutes
3. **Strategy** (entries 2-5) — cheap to absorb, prevents unforced errors
4. **MCQ + subjective** (entries 18-23) — worth a single focused pass, not more

## How to work through it

Do not read this section end to end like a book. Instead:

- Read entries 2-6 once. They take fifteen minutes total and change how you'll spend the two hours.
- For each archetype in 7-11, **build it from a blank file before reading the reference implementation.** Time yourself. Reading a solution you didn't attempt teaches you almost nothing about what you'll fumble at minute 70 of a real test.
- Use the linked drills to make the sub-skills automatic. A drill you can pass in three minutes is a drill you won't lose ten minutes to on test day.

## What "ready" looks like

You can build any of the five archetypes from an empty file in under 30 minutes, with loading / error / empty states, without looking anything up. That's the bar. Everything else in this section supports that one goal.

## Related

- [Decoding the Test Format](/test-prep/2) — what each question type actually is
- [The Five Archetypes](/test-prep/6) — the core of the section
- [React Interview Mastery Guide](/react-guide/1) — the deeper reference this section links into

learnings.title: Decoding the Test Format
learnings.answer:
Three question types, wildly different point values. Knowing which is which changes how you allocate two hours.

## MCQ

Standard multiple choice, auto-graded, instant. Topics skew to JavaScript fundamentals with some CSS and React mixed in. Usually 2-5 of them on a test this size, worth a handful of points each.

**Strategy:** answer fast, flag anything that takes more than 45 seconds, move on. There is no partial credit and no bonus for certainty.

## Subjective

**This is a question *type*, not a claim about the content.** "Subjective" on HackerEarth means: free-text answer box, no auto-grader, a human reads it. It is their counterpart to "MCQ" and "Project."

That matters because most subjective prompts have objectively correct answers. "Explain reflow vs repaint" is not a matter of opinion — it's only "subjective" in the sense that a person, not a test runner, decides whether you got it right.

What the grading mechanic implies:

- **A human skims it.** Structure and correct terminology are what get read.
- **Length is a trap.** Two tight paragraphs beat a page. Graders work from a rubric with a few key points and they're scanning for those words.
- **There's no completion signal.** Unlike a code question where tests tell you when you're done, this can absorb unlimited time. Budget ~10 minutes and stop.

Genuinely open-ended prompts do appear here too — "how would you architect a component library for a team of 20", "how would you debug a page that's slow on mobile." Those reward showing tradeoff reasoning. But the slot mostly gets used for knowledge questions that don't fit multiple choice.

## Project

A working UI, built in their in-browser IDE, with a live preview. This is the test. Everything else is rounding error.

Often partially **auto-graded against DOM assertions**, which is why prescribed `id` / `class` / `data-testid` names in the prompt are mandatory rather than suggestions. See [the IDE field notes](/test-prep/4).

## The point math

| Type | Typical count | Share of score |
|---|---|---|
| MCQ | 2-5 | ~5% |
| Subjective | 1 | ~7% |
| Project | 1-2 | **~88%** |

A perfect score on every MCQ and a blank project is a fail. A working project and three wrong MCQs is a pass. Plan accordingly.

## Related

- [The 2-Hour Time Budget](/test-prep/3)
- [Subjective Answers: The Structure That Scores](/test-prep/21)

learnings.title: The 2-Hour Time Budget
learnings.answer:
The single most common way to fail this test is to spend 40 minutes on the cheap questions and then run out of clock on the expensive one.

## The budget

| Segment | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Read every question first | 5 min | Know what's coming before you commit |
| **Project** | **80 min** | Start here if the UI lets you jump |
| MCQs | 8 min | Flag and move, never agonize |
| Subjective | 10 min | Bulleted, not prose |
| Final run + submit | 12 min | Non-negotiable buffer |
| Slack | 5 min | Something always goes wrong |

## Why project-first

The MCQs will still be there at minute 100. A half-finished project at minute 120 is where the points die. If the interface forces sequential answering, do the MCQs at speed — genuinely 90 seconds each, guess and flag anything slower — and get to the project.

## Inside the 80 project minutes

| Phase | Time | What you're doing |
|---|---|---|
| Read + identify archetype | 5 min | Match it to [one of the five](/test-prep/6). Note every prescribed selector name. |
| Scaffold | 5 min | Type [the skeleton](/test-prep/12) — state, container, render shell |
| Happy path | 30 min | Get the main flow rendering real data |
| States | 15 min | Loading, error, **empty**. These are graded and routinely skipped. |
| Polish + edge cases | 15 min | Validation, keyboard, the fiddly bits |
| Self-review against the prompt | 10 min | Re-read the spec line by line, tick each requirement |

That last 10 minutes is the highest-value time in the whole test. Requirements you simply forgot are the cheapest points on the table and the easiest to lose.

## Rules under pressure

- **Never debug for more than 5 minutes without changing approach.** Comment it out, ship the rest, come back.
- **Working and ugly beats elegant and broken.** No one grades your abstractions. They grade whether it runs.
- **Do not refactor.** Whatever you wrote at minute 30 is fine.
- **Save and run every few minutes.** Sessions drop. See [the IDE field notes](/test-prep/4).

## Related

- [The Last 12 Minutes](/test-prep/5) — the submission checklist
- [The Scaffold You Type First](/test-prep/12)

learnings.title: The In-Browser IDE: Field Notes
learnings.answer:
Things about HackerEarth's editor that are much better to learn now than at minute 10 of the test.

## What it is

A browser-based editor with a file tree, a **Run** button, and a live preview pane. Some questions ship a prebuilt starter — either vanilla HTML/CSS/JS or a React scaffold.

## What it is not

- **Not VS Code.** Autocomplete is weak or absent. IntelliSense will not save you from a misremembered method name. This is why [the cold-recall entries](/test-prep/13) exist.
- **Not npm.** You generally *cannot* install packages. Whatever is in `package.json` is what you get — usually just React and ReactDOM, sometimes nothing at all. No lodash, no axios, no date-fns, no UI library. Plan on `fetch` and standard library only.
- **Not fast.** It gets laggy on large files. Another reason not to write a 600-line component.

## The selector-name rule

This is the highest-value paragraph in this section.

If the prompt specifies an `id`, `class`, or `data-testid` — **use it exactly.** Auto-graders assert against the DOM:

```javascript
// The grader is doing something like this:
document.querySelector('[data-testid="user-list"]')
container.querySelectorAll('.item-row').length
```

Rename `item-row` to `itemRow` because it looks tidier and you score zero on that assertion no matter how well the feature works. Renaming prescribed selectors is the single most common way people bleed points on this test.

When the prompt shows sample markup, mirror its structure too — element types and nesting, not just class names.

## Practical habits

- **Save and Run every few minutes.** Sessions drop, tabs crash, and unsaved work is gone.
- **Check the preview pane early.** Confirm the starter actually runs *before* you write 100 lines against it.
- **console.log freely, but open the real browser console** — the embedded one is often truncated.
- **Don't trigger `alert()` / `confirm()`.** Modal dialogs can freeze the preview iframe.
- **Keep it to few files.** Multi-file refactors cost navigation time you don't have.
- **Don't paste from an online IDE.** The instructions explicitly prohibit external development environments, and they mean it.

## Before you write a line

1. Open every file in the starter. Know what exists.
2. Click Run. Confirm the baseline works.
3. Note the React version if there is one — hooks vs class components, whether `createRoot` or `ReactDOM.render`.
4. Copy every prescribed selector name into a comment at the top of your file. Tick them off as you go.

## Related

- [The 2-Hour Time Budget](/test-prep/3)
- [The Last 12 Minutes](/test-prep/5)

learnings.title: The Last 12 Minutes: Submission Checklist
learnings.answer:
Reserve these minutes. Do not spend them writing a feature. This is where recovered points live.

## The checklist

**Re-read the prompt, line by line.** Not skimmed — read. For each stated requirement, point at the code that satisfies it. This catches the "oh, it also said sort descending by default" class of mistake, which is pure free points.

**Verify every prescribed selector.** Search your code for each `data-testid` / `id` / `class` the prompt named. Exact spelling, exact case. See [the IDE field notes](/test-prep/4).

**Click Run one final time.** Confirm no console errors. A red console can fail assertions that would otherwise pass.

**Exercise the three states manually:**

- Loading — does something render while data is in flight?
- Error — kill the URL or throw, does it degrade gracefully instead of white-screening?
- Empty — search for `zzzzz`, does it say "no results" instead of rendering nothing?

**Test the boundaries.** Empty input. Single item. Last page of pagination. Rapid clicking. These are where auto-graders poke.

**Remove debug noise.** Stray `console.log`, commented-out experiments, unused state. Costs nothing to clean, and a human may read this.

**Confirm it's actually saved and submitted.** Not just Run — submitted. The instructions warn against closing the tab before final submission for a reason.

## If you're out of time and it's incomplete

Ship what works. A partially complete project that runs scores far better than a complete one that throws on load. Concretely:

- Comment out the broken feature rather than leaving it crashing the render.
- Make sure the app still mounts.
- If there's a notes field, one line: "Sorting implemented, pagination in progress" — a human grader may credit it.

## What not to do with these minutes

Don't start a new feature. Don't refactor for elegance. Don't rename things. Every one of those has a nonzero chance of breaking something that currently works, and you no longer have the clock to recover.

## Related

- [The 2-Hour Time Budget](/test-prep/3)

learnings.title: The Five Project Archetypes
learnings.answer:
Frontend take-home and timed project questions are remarkably repetitive. Nearly every one is a variation on five patterns. Recognizing yours in the first 90 seconds tells you what to scaffold.

## The five

| # | Archetype | Tell-tale wording | Entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fetch + search + filter | "fetch from this API", "search box", "filter by" | [7](/test-prep/7) |
| 2 | Sortable paginated table | "table", "sort by column", "page size", "pagination" | [8](/test-prep/8) |
| 3 | Form with validation | "form", "validate", "show error messages", "disable submit" | [9](/test-prep/9) |
| 4 | Stateful widget | "cart", "todo", "rating", "accordion", "tabs", "autocomplete" | [10](/test-prep/10) |
| 5 | Timer / carousel | "countdown", "stopwatch", "auto-advance", "every N seconds" | [11](/test-prep/11) |

## Identifying yours

Read the prompt once and ask three questions:

1. **Where does the data come from?** A network call → archetype 1. A provided array → 2, 3, or 4. Nothing, it's generated → 5.
2. **What's the primary interaction?** Typing to narrow a list → 1. Clicking headers / pages → 2. Filling fields → 3. Adding/removing/toggling items → 4. Watching it change on its own → 5.
3. **Is there a clock?** Any mention of intervals, delays, or auto-advance drags in archetype 5's concerns even if the surface looks like something else.

Combinations are common — "fetch a list, put it in a sortable table with search" is 1 + 2. That's fine. The archetypes compose; scaffold for the outer one and layer the inner.

## What every archetype is graded on

Regardless of which one you get, these show up in the rubric:

- **Loading state.** Something visible while data is in flight.
- **Error state.** A failed request must not white-screen the app.
- **Empty state.** Zero results needs its own message. This is the most-skipped requirement in the whole test.
- **Keys on lists.** `key={item.id}`, never the array index when the list can reorder. See [Reconciliation](/react-guide/4).
- **No console errors.** Auto-graders notice.
- **Prescribed selectors.** [Exactly as written.](/test-prep/4)

Build those six into your muscle memory and you clear the bar on any archetype.

## Related

- [The Scaffold You Type First](/test-prep/12) — one skeleton that fits all five

learnings.title: MCQ Hit-List: JavaScript
learnings.answer:
The MCQs skew heavily to JavaScript fundamentals. These are the topics that actually recur, each with the one thing you need to hold in your head, and links to practice in this app.

## Event loop and ordering

The rule: **all microtasks drain before the next macrotask.**

```javascript
console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);          // macrotask
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3')); // microtask
console.log('4');
// 1, 4, 3, 2
```

Microtasks: promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`, `await` continuations.
Macrotasks: `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O.

**Practice:** [/mcq/2](/mcq/2), [/mcq/30](/mcq/30), [/mcq/102](/mcq/102), [/mcq/133](/mcq/133) · output prediction [/output/4](/output/4), [/output/5](/output/5), [/output/6](/output/6), [/output/43](/output/43)

## Closures

A function keeps a live reference to the scope it was created in — not a copy.

```javascript
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 3 3 3
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 0 1 2
```

`var` is function-scoped, so all three callbacks share one binding. `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration.

**Practice:** [/mcq/76](/mcq/76), [/mcq/177](/mcq/177)

## Hoisting and the TDZ

`var` declarations hoist and initialize to `undefined`. `let` and `const` hoist but stay in the temporal dead zone — accessing them throws `ReferenceError`. Function declarations hoist entirely; function *expressions* do not.

**Practice:** [/mcq/1](/mcq/1), [/mcq/111](/mcq/111), [/mcq/163](/mcq/163), [/mcq/168](/mcq/168), [/mcq/171](/mcq/171)

## The `this` binding

Determined by *call site*, not definition site — except for arrow functions, which have no `this` and inherit from the enclosing scope lexically.

| Call form | Value of `this` |
|---|---|
| `obj.method()` | `obj` |
| `fn()` | `undefined` (strict) / `globalThis` (sloppy) |
| `new Fn()` | the new instance |
| `fn.call(x)` / `.apply` / `.bind` | `x` |
| arrow function | enclosing scope's `this` |

This is the largest topic in the bank — 156 tagged questions. **Practice:** [/mcq/3](/mcq/3), [/mcq/9](/mcq/9), [/mcq/10](/mcq/10) · [/output/48](/output/48), [/output/53](/output/53), [/output/63](/output/63)

## Coercion and equality

`==` coerces, `===` doesn't. Use `===` always; know `==` for the quiz.

```javascript
0 == '';            // true
null == undefined;  // true
null === undefined; // false
NaN === NaN;        // false — use Object.is or Number.isNaN
[] + {};            // "[object Object]"
typeof null;        // "object" (a famous bug)
```

Falsy values, all eight: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, the empty string, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `[]` and `{}`.

**Practice:** [/mcq/4](/mcq/4), [/mcq/15](/mcq/15), [/mcq/35](/mcq/35), [/mcq/41](/mcq/41)

## Prototypes

Property lookup walks the prototype chain. `Object.create(proto)`, `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`, and `class` as sugar over the same mechanism.

**Practice:** [/mcq/11](/mcq/11), [/mcq/14](/mcq/14), [/mcq/28](/mcq/28), [/mcq/55](/mcq/55)

## Also tagged heavily in the bank

- **Scope** (43 questions) — [/mcq/2](/mcq/2), [/mcq/20](/mcq/20), [/mcq/23](/mcq/23)
- **Map / Set** (39) — [/mcq/24](/mcq/24), [/mcq/29](/mcq/29), [/mcq/46](/mcq/46)
- **Generators** (29) — [/mcq/13](/mcq/13), [/mcq/16](/mcq/16), [/mcq/21](/mcq/21)
- **Spread / rest** (16) — [/mcq/19](/mcq/19), [/mcq/43](/mcq/43), [/mcq/60](/mcq/60)
- **Async / await** (6) — [/mcq/73](/mcq/73), [/mcq/124](/mcq/124), [/mcq/130](/mcq/130), [/mcq/152](/mcq/152)

## Related

- [MCQ Hit-List: CSS](/test-prep/19) · [MCQ Hit-List: React](/test-prep/20)

learnings.title: MCQ Hit-List: CSS
learnings.answer:
Fewer CSS questions than JavaScript, but they're quick points if you know the rules cold.

## Specificity

Count `(inline, id, class, element)`, compare left to right:

| Selector | Score |
|---|---|
| `div` | 0,0,0,1 |
| `.card` | 0,0,1,0 |
| `#header` | 0,1,0,0 |
| inline style attribute | 1,0,0,0 |
| `#a .b p` | 0,1,1,1 |

A single id beats any number of classes. `!important` overrides everything except another `!important` with higher specificity. Ties go to whichever comes last in source order.

`:is()` and `:not()` take the specificity of their most specific argument; `:where()` always contributes zero.

## Box model

```css
box-sizing: content-box; /* default: width = content only */
box-sizing: border-box;  /* width includes padding + border */
```

With `content-box`, an element with `width: 100px; padding: 20px; border: 5px` occupies **150px**. This is a classic MCQ.

Margins collapse vertically between siblings — adjacent 20px and 30px margins produce 30px of gap, not 50px. Horizontal margins never collapse, and collapsing is prevented by padding, borders, or a new formatting context.

## Positioning

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `static` | Default. `top`/`left` do nothing. |
| `relative` | Offset from its normal position; still occupies original space. |
| `absolute` | Removed from flow; positioned against nearest positioned ancestor. |
| `fixed` | Against the viewport (unless an ancestor has `transform`/`filter`). |
| `sticky` | Relative until a scroll threshold, then fixed. |

## Flexbox

```css
display: flex;
flex-direction: row;        /* main axis is horizontal */
justify-content: center;    /* along the MAIN axis */
align-items: center;        /* along the CROSS axis */
flex: 1;                    /* = flex: 1 1 0% */
gap: 16px;
```

The reliable trap: `justify-content` and `align-items` swap meaning when `flex-direction: column`. Perfect centering is `justify-content: center; align-items: center` in either direction.

## Grid

```css
display: grid;
grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));
grid-column: span 2;
gap: 16px;
```

`1fr` is a fraction of *remaining* space. `auto-fill` keeps empty tracks; `auto-fit` collapses them.

## Stacking context

`z-index` only works on positioned elements (or flex/grid children). A new stacking context is created by `position` plus `z-index`, and also by `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `will-change`, and `isolation: isolate`. A child can never escape its parent's stacking context — a `z-index: 9999` inside a context with `z-index: 1` still sits below a sibling context with `z-index: 2`.

## Units

`px` absolute · `em` relative to the element's font-size (compounds when nested) · `rem` relative to root · `%` relative to parent · `vw`/`vh` viewport · `ch` character width.

## Related

- [Subjective Answer Bank](/test-prep/22) — reflow vs repaint lives there

learnings.title: MCQ Hit-List: React
learnings.answer:
The React MCQs in this app are ids 232-245. These are the concepts they test.

## Rules of Hooks

Call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook only — never inside conditions, loops, or nested functions. React matches hooks to state by *call order*, so a conditional hook shifts every subsequent hook to the wrong slot.

Full explanation: [Rules of Hooks](/react-guide/12) · [How useState Actually Works](/react-guide/6)

**Practice:** [/mcq/232](/mcq/232), [/mcq/233](/mcq/233), [/mcq/235](/mcq/235), [/mcq/240](/mcq/240), [/mcq/245](/mcq/245)

## Keys and reconciliation

Keys tell React which element is which across renders. With index keys, removing the first of three items makes React think the *last* one disappeared and reuse the wrong DOM nodes — visible as focus jumping, wrong checkbox states, or lost input values.

Deeper: [Reconciliation](/react-guide/4)

## What triggers a re-render

A state update, a parent re-rendering, or a context value changing. **Not** mutating an object in place — `items.push(x)` followed by `setItems(items)` passes the same reference and React bails out.

Deeper: [What Actually Triggers a Re-render](/react-guide/14)

## Batching

React 18 batches all updates in the same tick, including inside promises and timeouts. Three `setState` calls in one handler produce one render.

```javascript
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);    // both read the same stale count — net +1

setCount((c) => c + 1);
setCount((c) => c + 1); // functional form — net +2
```

## Effects

`useEffect` runs after paint (async); `useLayoutEffect` runs before paint (sync, blocks). Use the layout variant only when you must measure the DOM and adjust before the user sees a flash.

The cleanup function runs before the next effect run *and* on unmount.

Deeper: [useEffect vs useLayoutEffect](/react-guide/8) · [StrictMode's Double-Invoke Behavior](/react-guide/33)

## Memoization

`React.memo` skips re-render when props are shallow-equal. It's defeated by a new object or inline arrow prop on every parent render — which is why `useCallback` and `useMemo` exist.

Deeper: [useMemo & useCallback](/react-guide/9) · [React.memo and the Reference Trap](/react-guide/15)

**Practice:** performance questions [/mcq/236](/mcq/236), [/mcq/241](/mcq/241)

## Controlled vs uncontrolled

Controlled: React state owns the value (`value` plus `onChange`). Uncontrolled: the DOM owns it (`defaultValue` plus a ref). Passing `value` without `onChange` produces a read-only input and a console warning.

Deeper: [Controlled vs. Uncontrolled](/react-guide/22)

## Context

Every consumer re-renders when the provider's value changes — including when you pass a fresh object literal each render.

Deeper: [Context Re-renders](/react-guide/28)

## Related

- [React Interview Mastery Guide](/react-guide/1) — the full reference
- [Subjective Answer Bank: React](/test-prep/23) — written answers for these topics
- [Gotcha Bank — 15 Rapid Answers](/react-guide/37)

learnings.title: Subjective Answers: The Structure That Scores
learnings.answer:
One free-text question, human-graded, roughly 10 minutes of your budget. The grader is working from a rubric of a few key points and skimming for them.

## The structure

**1. Answer sentence.** Directly, in one line. No warm-up, no "That's a great question," no restating the prompt.

**2. Three or four bullets.** The substance. One idea each, concrete, using the correct technical terms — those terms are literally what the rubric lists.

**3. One tradeoff or caveat line.** This is what separates a competent answer from a senior-sounding one. Show you know when the answer doesn't apply.

## Worked example

> **Prompt:** "How would you improve the performance of a page that renders a list of 10,000 items?"

> Render only what's visible — virtualize the list so the DOM holds a few dozen nodes instead of ten thousand.
>
> - **Windowing.** Render only rows in the viewport plus a small overscan buffer, translating a spacer element to preserve scroll height. This is the single biggest win: DOM node count drops by ~99%.
> - **Stable keys and memoized rows.** Give each row a stable id key and wrap it in `React.memo` so scrolling doesn't re-render untouched rows.
> - **Move work out of render.** Memoize filtering and sorting with `useMemo` so they don't rerun on unrelated state changes.
> - **Paginate at the source.** If the API supports it, fetching 50 rows at a time beats optimizing the rendering of 10,000.
>
> Tradeoff: virtualization complicates find-in-page, anchor links, and variable-height rows. For a few hundred items it's not worth the complexity — pagination is simpler and usually enough.

That's about 150 words and hits every rubric point. It took four minutes.

## Rules

- **Budget 10 minutes and stop.** There's no completion signal on a free-text box; it will absorb whatever you give it.
- **Bullets over prose.** Graders skim. A wall of text hides your correct answers.
- **Name things precisely.** "Reflow" not "the layout thing." "Microtask queue" not "the promise queue." The rubric contains terms.
- **Code only if it clarifies.** A four-line snippet can beat a paragraph. A forty-line one won't be read.
- **Don't hedge.** "It depends" as an opening reads as not knowing. Commit, then qualify in the tradeoff line.

## If you don't know the answer

Write what you *do* know, structured the same way, and be explicit about the boundary: "I'd approach this by X; I haven't worked with Y directly but I'd expect it to Z." Partial credit is real when a human grades. A blank box scores zero.

learnings.answer:
Model answers for the prompts that actually recur, in the [structure that scores](/test-prep/21).

## "Explain reflow vs repaint"

Reflow recalculates geometry; repaint redraws pixels. Reflow is the expensive one because it forces repaint too.

- **Repaint** happens when a change affects appearance but not layout — `color`, `background`, `visibility`, `box-shadow`. The browser redraws the affected pixels.
- **Reflow (layout)** happens when geometry changes — `width`, `height`, `padding`, `font-size`, adding or removing DOM nodes. The browser recomputes positions and sizes, potentially for the whole subtree or document.
- **Layout thrashing** is the pathological case: writing to the DOM then reading a layout property (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`) in a loop forces a synchronous reflow on every iteration.
- **Avoiding both:** animate `transform` and `opacity`, which are composited on the GPU and skip layout and paint entirely. Batch DOM reads before writes. Build off-DOM with a `DocumentFragment`.

Tradeoff: promoting elements to their own compositor layer (via `transform` or `will-change`) costs GPU memory, so applying it broadly can make things slower rather than faster.

## "How would you optimize a slow list?"

See the worked example in [the previous entry](/test-prep/21) — virtualize, memoize rows, move work out of render, paginate at the source.

Deeper: [Virtualizing Big Lists](/react-guide/16)

## "A page is slow on mobile. How do you debug it?"

Measure before changing anything — the bottleneck is rarely where you'd guess.

- **Profile first.** Lighthouse on a throttled 4G and 4x CPU profile, then the Performance panel to see whether time goes to network, script, layout, or paint. Test on a real mid-range device; desktop throttling flatters you.
- **Network.** Check payload size and request count. Usual wins: compress and resize images, serve modern formats, code-split the JS bundle, lazy-load below-the-fold content, add caching headers.
- **Main thread.** Look for long tasks over 50ms. Break them up, move heavy computation to a Web Worker, debounce expensive handlers.
- **Rendering.** Check for layout thrashing and unnecessary re-renders. On mobile, animating anything other than `transform`/`opacity` is usually visible jank.
- **Metrics to target.** LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1.

Tradeoff: aggressive code-splitting adds round trips, which can hurt on high-latency mobile networks. Fewer, larger chunks sometimes beat many small ones.

Deeper: ["The App Is Slow" — The Interview Playbook](/react-guide/18)

## "CSR vs SSR — when would you use each?"

Server-render when first paint and SEO matter; client-render when the app is interaction-heavy behind a login.

- **CSR** ships an empty shell plus JS. Slower first contentful paint, poor SEO without extra work, but cheap hosting and fast subsequent navigation.
- **SSR** returns rendered HTML per request. Fast FCP, works for crawlers, but needs a server and adds TTFB.
- **SSG** pre-renders at build time — fastest and cheapest, but only for content that doesn't change per request.
- **ISR and streaming** are the middle ground: static with periodic revalidation, or progressive HTML flush.

Tradeoff: SSR adds real operational complexity — a server to run, hydration mismatches to debug, and `window`-touching code that breaks on the server. For an internal dashboard behind auth, CSR is usually the right call.

Deeper: [CSR / SSR / SSG / ISR](/react-guide/29)

## "How do you make an application accessible and responsive?"

Often asked as two separate prompts. If you get both together, split your answer with subheadings — graders tick rubric lines, and subheadings make the ticks findable.

Accessibility comes from semantic HTML and keyboard support; responsiveness from fluid layout and relative units. Both are far cheaper designed in than retrofitted.

**Accessibility**

- **Semantic elements first.** A `<button>` is focusable, keyboard-activatable, and announced correctly for free. A `<div>` with an onClick is none of those things. Reach for ARIA only when no native element expresses the semantics.
- **Keyboard.** Everything interactive reachable by Tab and operable by Enter or Space. Modals trap focus, restore it to the trigger on close, and close on Escape. Never remove focus outlines without a visible replacement.
- **Names and state.** Every input paired with `<label htmlFor>`; icon-only buttons get an `aria-label`. Communicate dynamic state with `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-invalid`, and announce async changes with `aria-live`.
- **Contrast** at 4.5:1 for body text, and never colour as the sole signal of meaning.

**Responsiveness**

- **Mobile-first** with min-width media queries, so the base styles are the constrained case.
- **Fluid layout** via flex and grid with `minmax()` and `auto-fit`, so content reflows without a thicket of breakpoints. Container queries where a component must adapt to its container rather than the viewport.
- **Relative units** (`rem`, `%`, `ch`) so the page respects the user's font-size setting; touch targets at least 44px; `prefers-reduced-motion` honoured.

**Testing both:** tab through with the mouse unplugged, run a screen reader over one flow, and zoom to 200% — that catches more than any automated tool.

Tradeoff: ARIA is easy to get wrong, and incorrect ARIA is worse than none because it overrides correct native semantics. When in doubt, use the native element. Full WCAG AA compliance is ongoing effort, and automated checkers catch only about a third of real issues.

Deeper: [Accessibility Essentials](/react-guide/35)

## "How would you structure a component library for a team of 20?"

This one is genuinely open-ended — the grader wants tradeoff reasoning, not a single right answer.

- **Layering.** Primitives (Button, Input) then composed patterns (SearchField, DataTable) then app-specific components that stay in the app, not the library.
- **Tokens, not hardcoded values.** Colors, spacing, and typography as CSS custom properties so theming is a variable swap rather than a rewrite.
- **API discipline.** Controlled by default, escape hatches via `className` and `forwardRef`, no leaking internal DOM structure. Prefer composition (compound components) over twenty boolean props.
- **Contribution model.** Versioned releases with a changelog, visual regression tests, and a documented deprecation policy so twenty people can move without breaking each other.

Tradeoff: a shared library is a coordination cost. Below a certain team size or product surface, copy-paste between apps genuinely beats maintaining a package.

Deeper: [Compound Components](/react-guide/21) · [Micro-Frontends & Architecture](/react-guide/36)

learnings.answer:
Four prompts that come up constantly for React roles, scripted in the [structure that scores](/test-prep/21). These are **answer templates**, deliberately short — each is what you'd actually type in eight minutes. The `Deeper` links go to the full explanations elsewhere in the app; read those to understand the material, read these to know what to write.

## "Explain useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo. When would you use each?"

All three are memoization at different levels: `useMemo` caches a **value**, `useCallback` caches a **function reference**, and `React.memo` skips a **component's re-render**.

- **`React.memo(Component)`** wraps a component so it re-renders only when its props change by shallow comparison. This is the one that actually prevents work.
- **`useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b])`** caches a computed value between renders. Two uses: a genuinely expensive computation, and keeping an object or array reference stable so a memoized child or a dependency array doesn't see a new value every render.
- **`useCallback(fn, deps)`** is the same thing for functions — literally `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. Needed because a function defined in a component body is a fresh reference on every render.
- **The connection that matters:** `useMemo` and `useCallback` mostly exist to *make `React.memo` work*. Wrapping a child in `memo` and then passing it `onClick={() => ...}` accomplishes nothing — the arrow is a new reference each render, so the shallow compare always fails.

Tradeoff: memoization isn't free. It costs a dependency comparison and retained memory on every render, and it adds noise. Applied reflexively to cheap components it's a net loss — measure with the Profiler first. The React Compiler is making most manual memoization unnecessary.

**The trap:** most candidates describe the three in isolation. The point that reads as senior is the *dependency between them* — the fourth bullet. Lead with it if you're short on time.

Deeper: [useMemo & useCallback](/react-guide/9) · [React.memo and the Reference Trap](/react-guide/15) · [React.memo & Custom Comparison](/react-learnings/13)

## "How would you optimize a React app with unnecessary re-renders?"

Profile first to find what's actually re-rendering, then fix the cause rather than blanket-wrapping components in `memo`.

- **Measure.** React DevTools Profiler with "highlight updates" shows which components render and why. Guessing here wastes the most time.
- **Move state down.** The most common cause is state living too high — a modal's open state in `App` re-renders the whole tree. Colocate state with the component that uses it.
- **Pass children as a prop.** A component that renders `{children}` doesn't re-render them when its own state changes, because those elements were created by the parent. This fixes many cases with zero memoization, and almost nobody mentions it.

  Deeper on both: [Intro to Re-renders](/advanced-react/1) and [Elements, Children as Props, and Re-renders](/advanced-react/2).
- **Fix context.** Every consumer re-renders when the provider value changes, including on a fresh object literal each render. Memoize the value and split one broad context into several narrow ones so a theme change doesn't re-render auth consumers.
- **Then memoize.** `React.memo` on expensive subtrees, with `useCallback`/`useMemo` on the props feeding them — the two only work together.

Tradeoff: re-renders are cheap by default and React is fast. Optimizing before measuring adds complexity for no user-visible gain, and over-memoization can cost more than the renders it prevents.

Deeper: [Optimizing a Slow React App](/react-learnings/14) · ["The App Is Slow" — The Interview Playbook](/react-guide/18) · [What Actually Triggers a Re-render](/react-guide/14) · [Context Re-renders](/react-guide/28)

## "Design the frontend architecture for an app displaying thousands of records"

Two principles: never send all of it to the browser, and never render all of what you did send.

- **Push work to the server.** Pagination, filtering, sorting, and search belong in the API. Prefer keyset (cursor) pagination over `OFFSET` — it stays fast at depth and doesn't skip rows when data shifts under the user.
- **Virtualize the view.** Render only rows in the viewport plus a small overscan buffer, with a spacer preserving scroll height. DOM node count drops from thousands to dozens.
- **Separate the data layer from the view layer.** A query and cache layer owns fetching, deduplication, and invalidation; components stay presentational. This is what keeps it maintainable past the first feature.
- **Normalize and derive.** Store records keyed by id and keep sort/filter as *derived* selectors over that store rather than duplicated arrays. One source of truth, no drift.
- **Debounce and abort.** Search debounced around 300ms, in-flight requests cancelled with `AbortController` so a slow early response can't overwrite a fast later one.

Tradeoff: virtualization complicates find-in-page, anchor links, and variable-height rows, and server-side everything means a round trip per interaction. For a few hundred rows, client-side filtering with plain pagination is simpler and fast enough.

Deeper: [Virtualizing Big Lists](/react-guide/16) · [Server State vs. Client State](/react-guide/27) · [Archetype 2: Sortable Paginated Table](/test-prep/8)

## "How would you implement authentication in a React application?"

Store tokens in httpOnly cookies, keep access tokens short-lived, and treat client-side route guards as UX rather than security.

- **Token storage.** `httpOnly; Secure; SameSite` cookies, not `localStorage` — anything in `localStorage` is readable by any XSS on the page. Short-lived access token (~15 minutes) plus a longer refresh token with rotation.
- **Refresh flow.** An interceptor catches a 401, calls the refresh endpoint once, retries the original request, and queues concurrent requests so a burst of 401s doesn't fire N refreshes. If refresh fails, clear state and redirect to login.
- **App structure.** An auth context exposing `user`, `login`, `logout`, and a loading flag; a `ProtectedRoute` wrapper that redirects unauthenticated users and preserves the intended destination for post-login return.
- **The security boundary is the server.** Route guards and conditional rendering only hide UI. Every endpoint must authorize independently — a user can call the API directly.
- **Logout** clears the cookie server-side and resets client state, and ideally invalidates the refresh token so it can't be replayed.

Tradeoff: cookies bring CSRF exposure, mitigated with `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` plus a CSRF token, and they're awkward across domains. Holding the token in memory only (never persisted) avoids both but loses the session on refresh.

**This is the one where a wrong answer is actively penalized.** "Store the JWT in localStorage" is a common answer and reads as a security gap. Say the words *httpOnly*, *XSS*, and *short-lived* — they are almost certainly on the rubric.
